questions.q: How does this lesson distinguish an architecture principle from a one-off decision?
options: A principle is a standing rule agreed in advance that consistently guides many future decisions; a one-off decision is made for a single specific feature or situation and isn't meant to generalize
They are the same thing, just at different project phases
A principle only applies to Apex code, while one-off decisions only apply to Flow
One-off decisions always override architecture principles automatically
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly contrasts a standing, reusable rule (principle) with a single-use choice made for one feature (one-off decision) using the declarative-default example versus a specific Flow-ordering choice.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why do architecture principles help teams resolve disagreements faster?
options: They eliminate the need for any discussion at all
They move the conversation from re-litigating a general philosophical question every time to a narrower question of whether a specific case meets an already-agreed bar
They require a Technical Architect's sign-off before every decision
They have no actual effect on how disagreements get resolved
questions.explain: An agreed principle like 'default declarative unless X' lets the team skip re-arguing the general merits each time and jump straight to the narrower question of whether this specific case meets the agreed bar.

questions.q: Which of these is given in this lesson as an example of a recurring architecture principle?
options: Bulkify everything by default, with no exceptions for 'it'll probably only run on one record'
Always build custom objects instead of using standard objects
Never document the reasoning behind a design decision
Add a new trigger to an object every time a new requirement appears
questions.explain: The lesson lists bulkify-by-default as a recurring principle, specifically because the 'it'll only run on one record' assumption is exactly the one a future data load or integration tends to violate.

questions.q: What does this lesson say makes a list of architecture principles functionally worthless?
options: Having fewer than three principles
A list so long nobody can recall it without looking it up, or principles that are violated routinely without consequence -- at that point they're decoration or a suggestion, not a real standard
Writing the principles down anywhere at all
Enforcing the principles during design review
questions.explain: The lesson argues principles only work if they're few enough to remember, written down somewhere consulted, and genuinely enforced -- a long, unenforced list is effectively decoration, not guidance.

questions.q: What should a team do, per this lesson, with a principle that is routinely violated without consequence?
options: Keep it exactly as-is indefinitely, regardless of whether it's followed
Either genuinely commit to enforcing it or honestly retire it, rather than let it linger as nominal, unenforced guidance
Add ten more principles to compensate
Immediately escalate every violation to the Technical Architect certification board
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly recommends choosing between real enforcement and honest retirement, rather than letting an unenforced principle linger as a technicality nobody actually follows.
